screens.title: Implementing CI/CD Pipelines with OpenShift Pipelines (Tekton)
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn why CI and CD are essential for cloud-native platforms and how OpenShift Pipelines, implemented with Tekton, lets you run those pipelines directly inside your cluster. We start with the core idea: CI is about frequently integrating changes and running automated builds and tests; CD ensures validated code is ready to deploy. OpenShift Pipelines maps those practices onto Kubernetes-native resources: Task for a unit of work, Pipeline to sequence tasks, PipelineRun to execute, and Triggers to automate based on webhooks. You'll see concrete YAML examples for a git-clone Task, an S2I build Task, a deploy Task, and how a Pipeline wires them together using shared workspaces. We'll also cover PipelineRun execution, common mistakes such as overly large Tasks, and important operational notes about ServiceAccounts and image scanning. By the end you should be able to design focused Tasks, compose them into a Pipeline, run a PipelineRun, and reason about automating it with Triggers. Think about a microservice you maintain: how could you split its build, test, and deploy steps into reusable Tasks?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives frame the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will understand the core principles of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery in a cloud-native context: why frequent merges, automated builds, and rapid, safe deployments matter for reliability and speed. Second, you will be able to explain the architecture and key Tekton components—Task, Pipeline, PipelineRun, and Trigger—and how they map to Kubernetes resources. Third, you will design and implement Task and Pipeline YAML to express build, test and deploy steps, including parameter and workspace usage so artifacts flow between steps. Finally, you will configure PipelineRuns and Triggers to execute pipelines manually or automatically from Git events, and integrate common steps like building, testing, scanning, and deploying. Each objective includes hands-on checkpoints so you can prove competency by running an example PipelineRun and interpreting results. Think of these objectives as both mental models and practical checks: by the end you'll be able to read Tekton YAML, compose reusable Tasks, and automate execution with Triggers in a real OpenShift project.

screens.title: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery in a cloud-native context
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery are practical habits backed by automation. Continuous Integration means developers merge changes frequently into a shared repository and run automated builds and tests to catch integration problems early. Continuous Delivery extends that discipline by ensuring code that passes validation is always in a releasable state, with automated steps to deploy to environments. In a cloud-native platform like OpenShift, pipelines run as containers and use cluster primitives for storage, secrets, and security. A concrete example: when a developer pushes a feature branch, a git-clone Task can retrieve the code, a build Task can produce a container image into the cluster registry, a test Task runs unit tests, and a deploy Task updates a deployment. This pipeline sequence shortens feedback loops and reduces human error. A common misconception is equating CD only with automatic production deploys; CD more precisely means the software is always releasable—teams may still gate production deployment. The practical takeaway is to design pipelines that provide fast feedback, are repeatable, and leverage OpenShift features like ImageStreams and routes for final verification. How would you split your current build process into smaller, testable steps?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › CI / CD Basics
Definition and value
Why teams adopt CI/CD and how OpenShift changes pipeline placement.
  • CI: frequent merges with automated builds and tests to find issues early.
  • CD: keep validated artifacts releasable and automate deployments as appropriate.
  • OpenShift Pipelines runs pipeline steps as containers, using cluster storage and security.
Concrete example
A developer pushes to main → git-clone Task retrieves code → build Task produces image → test Task runs unit tests → deploy Task updates the app.
Common misconception
CD does not always mean automatic production deploys. It means the codebase is always ready to be deployed with confidence.
Analogy
Treat each Task as a specialist worker on an assembly line; the Pipeline is the production line organizing the sequence.
Key takeaway
Design pipelines for fast feedback, small steps, and clear artifact flow so you can iterate safely.

screens.title: Tekton Resources: Task
screens.narratorSegment: A Tekton Task is the smallest executable unit in a pipeline. It encapsulates an ordered set of steps; each step runs in its own container image and performs a single part of the work. Tasks are intended to be reusable and parameterized, so you can use the same Task for different repositories or branches by passing parameters. The Task also declares Workspaces to read or write files shared across steps and Results to emit small pieces of data such as an image digest. A practical example from the chapter is a git-clone Task that accepts a url and revision parameter, uses a container with git, clones into the workspace, and checks out the requested revision. When you design Tasks, aim for single responsibility: cloning, building, testing and deploying should normally be separate Tasks. A common pitfall is creating huge Tasks that perform many unrelated steps; that reduces reuse and complicates debugging. As a closing check, think how you would parameterize a build Task to accept a builder image and an image name—this enables reuse across projects and branches. Tekton Resources: Task means tasks run steps in containers, accept parameters and workspaces, and should be small and reusable.. In practical terms, what a task is, parameters, steps, and a git-clone example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Task
Tekton Task explained
Parameters, workspaces, steps and Results are the building blocks.
  • Params allow Tasks to be reused for different inputs like URL or revision.
  • Workspaces are mounted volumes shared across steps in a Task or Pipeline.
  • Results are small outputs a Task can write for later consumption.
git-clone example
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: git-clone
spec:
  params:
    - name: url
      type: string
    - name: revision
      type: string
      default: main
  workspaces:
    - name: output
  steps:
    - name: clone
      image: registry.redhat.io/openshift-pipelines/tkn-cli:latest
      script: |
        #!/usr/bin/env bash
        set -eu
        git clone "$(params.url)" "$(workspaces.output.path)"
        cd "$(workspaces.output.path)"
        git checkout "$(params.revision)"
Design guidance
Aim for small Tasks with a single responsibility so they remain reusable across Pipelines.
Common pitfall
Avoid monolithic Tasks that both build and deploy. That reduces reuse and makes troubleshooting harder.
Concrete check
Parameterize your git-clone Task and run it with different URLs to verify reuse.

screens.title: Tekton Resources: Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: A Pipeline orchestrates Tasks by declaring the sequence of steps, their parameters, and how they share files and results. Pipelines bind Tasks using taskRef and can express ordering with runAfter. To move artifacts between Tasks, Pipelines declare Workspaces which become mounted volumes available to each Task that needs them; this is how a git clone can populate a shared workspace that a build Task later consumes. Results are small named outputs a Task writes, like an image digest or test summary; later Tasks or external tooling can read these results. The chapter example shows a Pipeline named app-build-deploy-pipeline that accepts parameters for git-url, git-revision, and image-name, defines a shared-workspace, and sequences fetch-repository then build-image then additional tasks. One misconception is assuming Results replace workspaces; Results are for tiny text values, not full file transfer. When designing Pipelines, make parameter intent explicit and use Workspaces for files and Results for metadata. Consider how you'd surface failures: use small Tasks so logs point to the failing step and Results to record success metadata for downstream automation. Tekton Resources: Pipeline means pipelines sequence tasks, bind workspaces to share files, and use results to emit small metadata between steps.. In practical terms, compose tasks, use workspaces and results to pass data between steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Pipeline
Pipeline structure
Parameters, Workspaces and task list form the Pipeline API surface.
Example snippet
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Pipeline
metadata:
  name: app-build-deploy-pipeline
spec:
  params:
    - name: git-url
      type: string
    - name: git-revision
      type: string
      default: main
  workspaces:
    - name: shared-workspace
  tasks:
    - name: fetch-repository
      taskRef:
        name: git-clone
      params:
        - name: url
          value: $(params.git-url)
      workspaces:
        - name: output
          workspace: shared-workspace
    - name: build-image
      runAfter: ["fetch-repository"]
      taskRef:
        name: buildah
      workspaces:
        - name: source
          workspace: shared-workspace
Notes and guidance
  • Use Workspaces for files and artifact passing, not Results.
  • Results are for short values like digests or test counts.
  • Explicit runAfter or task dependencies improve readability for complex Pipelines.
Key takeaway
Design Pipelines that clearly express data flow: which workspace holds sources, which Results matter, and how Tasks depend on each other.

screens.title: PipelineRun: executing a Pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: A PipelineRun is how you execute a Pipeline: it provides concrete parameter values, workspace bindings, and optionally a service account. Creating a PipelineRun instantiates the steps as pods in OpenShift which you can monitor using CLI tools. The chapter shows a PipelineRun that sets git-url, git-revision, and image-name, and binds a volumeClaimTemplate to the shared-workspace so the run has persistent storage for files. When the PipelineRun starts, you'll see pods for each Task step, their logs, and final status. Use tkn or oc to describe and follow the run. A common mistake is forgetting serviceAccount scopes—make sure the ServiceAccount assigned has only the permissions needed for the job, for example creating Deployments or ImageStreamTags but not cluster-admin. Another pitfall is missing workspace PVC sizing; a too-small PVC may cause failures. As a practical process, create the PipelineRun, watch step logs, and inspect created resources like ImageStreams and Deployments. End by asking: did the run produce the expected ImageStream tag and is the deployed route available? PipelineRun: executing a Pipeline means pipelinerun binds parameters and workspaces to execute a pipeline; monitor pods, logs, and resource outputs to validate the run.. In practical terms, how to instantiate a pipeline and observe its execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › PipelineRun
Create and monitor a PipelineRun
Provide concrete params, workspace PVCs, and optional serviceAccount.
PipelineRun example
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: PipelineRun
metadata:
  generateName: app-build-deploy-run-
spec:
  pipelineRef:
    name: app-build-deploy-pipeline
  params:
    - name: git-url
      value: https://github.com/myorg/myrepo.git
    - name: git-revision
      value: main
  workspaces:
    - name: shared-workspace
      volumeClaimTemplate:
        spec:
          accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
          resources:
            requests:
              storage: 1Gi
Monitoring tips
  • Use tkn pipelinerun describe and oc get pod -w to follow progress.
  • Inspect step logs to locate failures quickly.
  • Check ImageStream and Deployment objects after successful runs.
Common pitfalls
  • Missing ServiceAccount permissions lead to failing deploy steps.
  • Insufficient PVC size causes workspace writes to fail.
Check your run
After completion, confirm an ImageStreamTag was created and the application route is present if deployed.

screens.title: Triggers: automating pipeline execution from Git events
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers let you automate PipelineRuns in response to external events such as Git webhooks. The Tekton Trigger model uses three cooperating resources: an EventListener listens for incoming HTTP events; a TriggerBinding extracts values such as repository URL or branch from the payload; a TriggerTemplate uses those values to instantiate a PipelineRun. In practice you deploy an EventListener service in your cluster, configure your Git provider to call its endpoint on push events, and ensure TriggerBinding maps JSON fields to the parameters your Pipeline expects. The chapter explains that this creates a fully automated loop: developer pushes code, webhook fires, EventListener receives event, TriggerBinding extracts git-url and revision, TriggerTemplate generates a PipelineRun, and the pipeline executes. A commonly overlooked detail is secure exposure of the EventListener; use ingress and secret validation to avoid unauthorized runs. Also validate that your TriggerBinding extracts the correct JSON paths for your Git provider. To test, generate a manual webhook payload or use a test push to confirm a PipelineRun appears in the cluster. Ask yourself: how will you secure the listener and limit permissions for the ServiceAccount that runs triggered PipelineRuns?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Triggers
Trigger components
EventListener, TriggerBinding, TriggerTemplate—how they collaborate.
EventListener: receives webhook HTTP calls and routes events to configured triggers.
TriggerBinding: maps values from the event payload into parameters.
TriggerTemplate: creates the PipelineRun manifest using extracted values.
Security note
Protect EventListener endpoints and validate webhook signatures before creating PipelineRuns to prevent unauthorized executions.
Testing and validation
  • Send a sample webhook payload to the EventListener to confirm TriggerBinding extracts the right fields.
  • Confirm that a PipelineRun appears with expected params and workspace bindings.
Key takeaway: Automate carefully and secure the listener. Triggers complete the CI/CD loop by turning external events into pipeline executions.

screens.title: Workspaces and Results: passing artifacts and metadata
screens.narratorSegment: Workspaces and Results serve different purposes when passing information between Tasks. Workspaces are mounted volumes—suitable for full source trees, build artifacts, or any file-level data that one Task writes and another reads. Results are small strings or numbers that a Task writes to signal metadata like an image digest, test counts, or a version. Use Workspaces when you need files preserved across steps, and Results when you need concise values consumed by subsequent steps or reported. For example, the git-clone Task writes source files into a shared-workspace PVC. A build Task reads from that same workspace, produces an image, and writes a Result with the image digest. A downstream deploy Task can read that digest to tag or reference the image. A common mistake is attempting to put large binary artifacts into Results—they are not designed for that. Also be mindful of PVC sizing and accessModes. The practical pattern is: use a PVC-backed shared-workspace for sources, have build Tasks publish Results like digest or version, and keep Tasks small so the provenance of artifacts is clear. How would you record a test report and make it available to later steps or external reporting?

A downstream deploy Task can read that digest to tag or reference the image. A common mistake is attempting to put large binary artifacts into Results—they are not designed for that. Also be mindful of PVC sizing and accessModes. The practical pattern is: use a PVC-backed shared-workspace for sources, have build Tasks publish Results like digest or version, and keep Tasks small so the provenance of artifacts is clear. Workspaces: files and artifacts
PVC-backed volumes shared by Tasks within a PipelineRun.
Use a shared-workspace to move source code from git-clone to build tasks, or to store test reports and binaries across steps.
Results: metadata
Small text values written by Tasks for later consumption or reporting.

Practical patterns

screens.title: Best practices and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Design choices matter for pipelines. One best practice is Task granularity: keep Tasks focused on single responsibilities like cloning, building, testing, scanning, or deploying. This improves reuse across projects and makes failure analysis straightforward. Contrast that with a monolithic Task that does build, test and deploy in one container: it's harder to reuse and debug. Security is another essential area: ServiceAccounts used for PipelineRuns should have the least privilege necessary, for example permissions to create Deployments or ImageStreamTags in the project but not cluster-admin. Also incorporate image scanning early: add a scan Task near the start of your pipeline so vulnerabilities are found before deployment. A common pitfall is neglecting Result and Workspace hygiene: not emitting digests or not explicitly binding workspaces can produce non-reproducible runs. Operationally, make sure PVCs are sized and that logs from step pods are collected for troubleshooting. The practical advice is to codify these patterns into templates so teams get consistent, secure pipelines by default. content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Hands-on Pipeline
Hands-on pipeline YAML walkthrough
Follow these YAML steps in order and validate each Task with a TaskRun when possible.
s2i-app-build Task (excerpt)
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: s2i-app-build
spec:
  params:
    - name: SOURCE_PATH
    - name: APP_NAME
    - name: BUILDER_IMAGE
  workspaces:
    - name: source
  steps:
    - name: create-buildconfig
      image: registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cli:latest
      script: |
        #!/usr/bin/env bash
        set -eu
        if ! oc get buildconfig $(params.APP_NAME) &> /dev/null; then
          oc new-build --strategy=source --binary=true --name=$(params.APP_NAME) --image-stream=$(params.BUILDER_IMAGE)
        fi
deploy-app Task (excerpt)
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1beta1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: deploy-app
spec:
  params:
    - name: APP_NAME
    - name: IMAGE_STREAM_TAG
    - name: PORT
  steps:
    - name: deploy
      image: registry.redhat.io/openshift4/ose-cli:latest
      script: |
        #!/usr/bin/env bash
        set -eu
        if ! oc get deployment $(params.APP_NAME) &> /dev/null; then
          oc new-app $(params.IMAGE_STREAM_TAG) --name=$(params.APP_NAME) --port=$(params.PORT)
          oc expose service $(params.APP_NAME)
        else
          oc set image deployment/$(params.APP_NAME) $(params.APP_NAME)=$(params.IMAGE_STREAM_TAG) --dry-run=client -o yaml | oc apply -f -
        fi
Execution checklist
  • Ensure openshift-pipelines operator is installed and necessary Tasks are available.
  • Create project, bind ServiceAccount roles, apply Tasks and Pipeline YAML.
  • Create PipelineRun and monitor with tkn or oc. Verify ImageStream and route after completion.
Pro tip: validate each Task via a TaskRun before composing the full Pipeline so you localize issues quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn why CI and CD are essential for cloud-native platforms and how OpenShift Pipelines, implemented with Tekton, lets you run those pipelines directly inside your cluster. We start with the core idea: CI is about frequently integrating changes and running automated builds and tests; CD ensures validated code is ready to deploy. OpenShift Pipelines maps those practices onto Kubernetes-native resources: Task for a unit of work, Pipeline to sequence tasks, PipelineRun to execute, and Triggers to automate based on webhooks. You'll see concrete YAML examples for a git-clone Task, an S2I build Task, a deploy Task, and how a Pipeline wires them together using shared workspaces. We'll also cover PipelineRun execution, common mistakes such as overly large Tasks, and important operational notes about ServiceAccounts and image scanning. By the end you should be able to design focused Tasks, compose them into a Pipeline, run a PipelineRun, and reason about automating it with Triggers. Think about a microservice you maintain: how could you split its build, test, and deploy steps into reusable Tasks?

These learning objectives frame the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will understand the core principles of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery in a cloud-native context: why frequent merges, automated builds, and rapid, safe deployments matter for reliability and speed. Second, you will be able to explain the architecture and key Tekton components—Task, Pipeline, PipelineRun, and Trigger—and how they map to Kubernetes resources. Third, you will design and implement Task and Pipeline YAML to express build, test and deploy steps, including parameter and workspace usage so artifacts flow between steps. Finally, you will configure PipelineRuns and Triggers to execute pipelines manually or automatically from Git events, and integrate common steps like building, testing, scanning, and deploying. Each objective includes hands-on checkpoints so you can prove competency by running an example PipelineRun and interpreting results. Think of these objectives as both mental models and practical checks: by the end you'll be able to read Tekton YAML, compose reusable Tasks, and automate execution with Triggers in a real OpenShift project.

This second objectives slide focuses on how you'll demonstrate the skills. You'll author reusable Task YAML that each perform a single responsibility—cloning source, building an image, running tests, or deploying. Then you'll assemble those Tasks in a Pipeline that declares Workspaces for shared files and Results for small outputs like an image digest. To prove mastery, you'll run a PipelineRun that binds a PVC-backed workspace and specific parameters, inspect logs using CLI tooling, and observe the pods and steps that run in OpenShift. For automation, you'll configure an EventListener, TriggerBinding, and TriggerTemplate to create PipelineRuns from Git webhooks. We'll evaluate your outcomes by checking that the PipelineRun completes, that artifacts are available in the expected ImageStream or registry, and that the deployed app exposes a route. Each objective includes practical checks rather than theory alone: create the resources, trigger a run, and interpret logs. Remember, the goal is repeatable, observable pipelines that can be automated safely in production-like projects.

Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery are practical habits backed by automation. Continuous Integration means developers merge changes frequently into a shared repository and run automated builds and tests to catch integration problems early. Continuous Delivery extends that discipline by ensuring code that passes validation is always in a releasable state, with automated steps to deploy to environments. In a cloud-native platform like OpenShift, pipelines run as containers and use cluster primitives for storage, secrets, and security. A concrete example: when a developer pushes a feature branch, a git-clone Task can retrieve the code, a build Task can produce a container image into the cluster registry, a test Task runs unit tests, and a deploy Task updates a deployment. This pipeline sequence shortens feedback loops and reduces human error. A common misconception is equating CD only with automatic production deploys; CD more precisely means the software is always releasable—teams may still gate production deployment. The practical takeaway is to design pipelines that provide fast feedback, are repeatable, and leverage OpenShift features like ImageStreams and routes for final verification. How would you split your current build process into smaller, testable steps?

A Tekton Task is the smallest executable unit in a pipeline. It encapsulates an ordered set of steps; each step runs in its own container image and performs a single part of the work. Tasks are intended to be reusable and parameterized, so you can use the same Task for different repositories or branches by passing parameters. The Task also declares Workspaces to read or write files shared across steps and Results to emit small pieces of data such as an image digest. A practical example from the chapter is a git-clone Task that accepts a url and revision parameter, uses a container with git, clones into the workspace, and checks out the requested revision. When you design Tasks, aim for single responsibility: cloning, building, testing and deploying should normally be separate Tasks. A common pitfall is creating huge Tasks that perform many unrelated steps; that reduces reuse and complicates debugging. As a closing check, think how you would parameterize a build Task to accept a builder image and an image name—this enables reuse across projects and branches. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Pipeline orchestrates Tasks by declaring the sequence of steps, their parameters, and how they share files and results. Pipelines bind Tasks using taskRef and can express ordering with runAfter. To move artifacts between Tasks, Pipelines declare Workspaces which become mounted volumes available to each Task that needs them; this is how a git clone can populate a shared workspace that a build Task later consumes. Results are small named outputs a Task writes, like an image digest or test summary; later Tasks or external tooling can read these results. The chapter example shows a Pipeline named app-build-deploy-pipeline that accepts parameters for git-url, git-revision, and image-name, defines a shared-workspace, and sequences fetch-repository then build-image then additional tasks. One misconception is assuming Results replace workspaces; Results are for tiny text values, not full file transfer. When designing Pipelines, make parameter intent explicit and use Workspaces for files and Results for metadata. Consider how you'd surface failures: use small Tasks so logs point to the failing step and Results to record success metadata for downstream automation. A PipelineRun is how you execute a Pipeline: it provides concrete parameter values, workspace bindings, and optionally a service account. Creating a PipelineRun instantiates the steps as pods in OpenShift which you can monitor using CLI tools. The chapter shows a PipelineRun that sets git-url, git-revision, and image-name, and binds a volumeClaimTemplate to the shared-workspace so the run has persistent storage for files. Triggers let you automate PipelineRuns in response to external events such as Git webhooks. The Tekton Trigger model uses three cooperating resources: an EventListener listens for incoming HTTP events; a TriggerBinding extracts values such as repository URL or branch from the payload; a TriggerTemplate uses those values to instantiate a PipelineRun. In practice you deploy an EventListener service in your cluster, configure your Git provider to call its endpoint on push events, and ensure TriggerBinding maps JSON fields to the parameters your Pipeline expects. The chapter explains that this creates a fully automated loop: developer pushes code, webhook fires, EventListener receives event, TriggerBinding extracts git-url and revision, TriggerTemplate generates a PipelineRun, and the pipeline executes. A commonly overlooked detail is secure exposure of the EventListener; use ingress and secret validation to avoid unauthorized runs. Also validate that your TriggerBinding extracts the correct JSON paths for your Git provider. To test, generate a manual webhook payload or use a test push to confirm a PipelineRun appears in the cluster.
